Coming out of the Queens, New York high school ranks, Montesa began his college career with Division II Adelphi in his home state. He earned Northeast 10 Conference Pitcher of the Year honors as a sophomore, catching the attention of Division I programs. The right-hander transferred to West Virginia for his junior season and opened a lot of eyes early in the season to give himself some helium. He wasn’t able to maintain it consistently, especially in Big 12 play, but while he lost his rotation spot late in the year, scouts still liked his pure stuff enough to keep him in Day 2 conversations. Montesa is an athletic 6-foot-1 right-hander who has a four-pitch mix that could give him the chance to start at the next level. His fastball sits in the mid-90s and can touch 98 at times, and it’s a tough pitch to barrel -- with a decent amount of swing-and-miss -- when he’s up in the zone. Command of the pitch was iffy at best, and the heater can get hit when he’s down in the zone with it too much. He does have a very good feel for spin for both his preferred upper-70s curve that he can manipulate the shape of when he’s locked in and his lesser-thrown harder and shorter mid-80s slider, both of which miss plenty of bats. There is a firm upper-80s changeup in there as well, though it’s clearly his fourth pitch. The biggest thing holding Montesa back is his command. His walk rate climbed as the 2026 season wore on, and his 5.98 BB/9 rate in Big 12 play undoubtedly contributed to him being taken out of the rotation as postseason play loomed, though his good raw stuff and age (he’s still only 20 years old come Draft time) were enough for teams to be discussing in the top several rounds.

The best player to ever come out of Butler Area High School north of Pittsburgh is right-hander Matt Clement, a 1993 third-rounder who spent parts of nine years in the big leagues, but there hasn’t been a player drafted from the program since 2003. This year, the Golden Tornado have a pair of right-handed pitchers who have intrigued scouts. The scouting industry might have had Nolan Stefaniak ahead of Casteel entering the spring, but that’s likely flipped as the latter has made some big strides this spring. Casteel’s combination of size, projection and improved pitchability had teams running to western Pennsylvania to get more looks at him. The 6-foot-4 hurler typically sits around 92 mph and tops out at 95 mph, but he can maintain the low-90s velocity deep into starts, and it’s easy to dream about more to come as he fills out his frame. He has a slider that has the chance to be a true out pitch, mostly with three-quarters shape, depth and bite, though he can manipulate it into more of a slurve or a sweeper as he needs it. He doesn’t use his changeup much, but it has the chance to be a solid third offering with some fade. In addition to Casteel’s stuff ticking up, he also showed a better feel for finding the zone, with solid command and control compared to looks from the fall. The feel for pitching and pure arm strength point to some ceiling here, with some evaluators talking about the West Virginia recruit in the top five rounds.

The state of Georgia doesn't have its usual first-round high school pitcher in 2023, but the state's best mound prospect is extremely polished for his age and could factor into the top three rounds if he's signable. McNeillie hails from a Milton HS program that has spawned three significant big leaguers in Kyle Farnsworth, Dexter Fowler and Dylan Cease. He has a lot of upside and projection remaining and could develop into a first-rounder in '26 if he follows through on his college commitment to Florida. McNeillie's fastball currently parks at 88-91 mph and tops out at 94, but it plays better than its velocity. He uses both two-seamers and four-seamers while working all four quadrants of the strike zone, and his three-quarters delivery creates impressive life, angle and deception. He should throw harder once he adds some much-needed strength to his thin 6-foot-2 frame. McNeillie likes to attack hitters with his heater and will have to use his secondary pitches more often against more advanced hitters. He has the potential for three solid offerings as he achieves good sweep on a mid-70s slider and tough sink on a low-80s changeup. He has a quick arm and an easy, repeatable delivery that allow him to pound the strike zone.

Harris entered the start of the summer showcase circuit last year considered one of the best high school position players in the country. And he showed off glimpses of his considerable tools at nearly every event possible, including the Perfect Game National, both PG’s and MLB’s High School All-American Games, the East Coast Pro Showcase and the Area Code Game. With his skills, however, came some questions about his hit tool. When the Jacksonville, Florida prep standout continued to have swing-and-miss issues during his senior year, his Draft stock took a hit, leaving his status up in the air. At 6-foot-2 and hitting from the right side, he’s reminded some area scouts in Florida of a young Dylan Crews, who played his high school ball in Florida before heading to LSU. There is definite raw power in his game, and he can get to it at times when he keeps his barrel in the zone for a long time and creates leverage. But he has struggled to find consistency at the plate, with strikeouts still plaguing him this spring, especially having difficulty connecting against breaking stuff. Harris does have above-average speed and uses it well on both sides of the ball. When he combines it with his outstanding instincts in center field, he looks like a potentially plus defender up the middle in the future. The arm would play in a corner, and he might have the raw power to profile there if need be, but it might not be until he spends some years in the University of Florida lineup before he moves on to pro ball.

When Sosa first entered Viera HS (Fla.), he was around 5-foot-5 and weighed maybe 160 pounds, not exactly the kind of physique that screams future catching prospect. Four years and close to 7 inches and 40 pounds later, Sosa’s name has been steadily rising up Draft boards. He really put himself on the map during summer showcase circuit events like Perfect Game National, East Coast Pro and the Baseball Factory All-America Game Scouts love the combination of Sosa’s strong body, offensive potential, chance to stick behind the plate and blue-collar approach to the game. Teams love left-handed-hitting catchers, and Sosa has the chance to be a good one, showing an ability to control the zone well, drawing a ton of walks and rarely trying to do too much. He has a simple and repeatable swing and can handle righties and lefties. It’s more of a line-drive approach right now, but there’s solid raw power for him to tap into in the future. Sosa does show a little stiffness with too wide of a base behind the plate. That said, he does a decent job receiving and blocking, with the agility to improve on that front, and his arm is solid and accurate. The high school catching demographic is a risky one, but Sosa could be enticing enough to draft and sign away from his commitment to North Carolina State.

Hailing from Oakton High School in Virginia, Lavey stayed in the region to head to George Washington University to extend his baseball career. He made an immediate impact as a freshman, earning second-team All Atlantic 10 honors, repeating the feat again as a junior. In between, he was a Cape Cod League All-Star. His solid showing on the Cape, carrying that over to the 2026 season and constant need for decent all-around catchers had teams considering Lavey in the top several rounds. Lavey checks off an oft-coveted box as a left-handed-hitting catcher. Nothing he does is flashy, but he can do everything pretty well. He has an easy swing, with a line-drive, up the middle approach, and he has the strength to drive the ball at times, with solid exit velocity data to back that up. He doesn’t swing and miss or chase much and walked more than he struck out as a junior. Behind the plate, there’s work to be done, but he has the makings of a solid defensive backstop, one with an above-average arm and pop times under 2.00 seconds. He’d receive better instruction on his glove work on the pro side, so there’s some ceiling to reach there. That and his steady bat had some believing he could go in the top five rounds come Draft time.

Behind the plate, there’s work to be done, but he has the makings of a solid defensive backstop, one with an above-average arm and pop times under 2.00 seconds. He’d receive better instruction on his glove work on the pro side, so there’s some ceiling to reach there. That and his steady bat had some believing he could go in the top five rounds come Draft time.

Plant City HS, located between Tampa and Lakeland in Florida, has produced two big leaguers over the years. Both were left-handed pitchers: Kenny Rogers, who signed out of high school, and Parker Messick, who went on to Florida State before being drafted by the Guardians in 2022. Carbaugh might be right-handed, but he has the chance to be the first player drafted from the school since Rogers in 1982 after initially showing off his size and stuff at summer showcase events like the East Coast Pro Showcase and Perfect Game National, then continuing to miss bats during his senior season. Teams are likely to be intrigued by Carbaugh’s 6-foot-5 frame and potential three-pitch mix. He can crank his fastball up to 96 mph. It has two-seam characteristics, with more run than sink because he delivers it from a low slot. He has a slider, thrown around 80 mph, that has more sweep than tilt regularly. He hasn’t used his changeup much, but he has some feel for the low-80s offspeed offering. Considering his size, Carbaugh does a decent job of repeating his delivery and finding the strike zone, though it’s definitely control over command. The Mississippi State recruit reminds some scouts of 2024 prospect Dylan Jordan (who joined the Angels after receiving an over-slot deal in the fifth round that July), albeit without as much extension.

Thiel is one of the more projectable and most improved high school pitchers in the Midwest. The 6-foot-7 left-hander topped out at 88 mph during East Coast Pro tryout last summer and failed to make the team, but he has added about 5 mph to his fastball this spring. While many scouts believe he'd be best served by attending Ohio State and adding more strength and polish, there are enough interested teams that he may not get to Columbus. Thiel now reaches 94 mph early in games and operates at 89-91 mph throughout his starts, imparting carry and armside run on his heater. He gets good depth on a curveball that reaches the upper 70s and owns a slider with more power and horizontal action but less consistency. He also demonstrates feel for a changeup that parks around 80 mph and drops at the plate. After gaining significant strength during the last year, Thiel now carries 230 pounds on his tall frame and still has room to add more. He uses his size to create extension and angle that add deception. He throws more strikes than most teenage southpaws his size and projects to develop average control and command.

One of the biggest wild cards in the Draft, Jelkin got dismissed from Nebraska as a freshman in 2022 and teams are still wary of his makeup. He spent 2023 at South Mountain (Ariz.) CC before blowing out his elbow at Houston the following spring, requiring Tommy John surgery that sidelined him for all of last season at Kentucky. He turned down the Dodgers as a 14th-rounder in 2023 and the Mets as a ninth-rounder in '24. Though he'll be 23 years and seven months old on Draft Day, he also has top two rounds stuff and earned second-team All-Southeastern Conference honors as a redshirt senior. Jelkin operates with three solid pitches with high spin rates, the best of which is a low-80s curveball with quality depth. His fastball has sat at 93-96 mph and reached 98 with power sink this spring, and it touched 100 during fall practice. His upper-80s cutter features late break that keeps it off barrels. Jelkin also shows some aptitude for a mid-80s changeup with fade and sink. A lanky 6-foot-5, 195-pounder with room to add more strength, he slings his pitches from a low three-quarters slot that adds deception. While he provides consistent strikes, he does catch the heart of the plate too often and will need to upgrade his command.

American Heritage HS in Plantation, Fla., has produced a good amount of big league talent, from Eric Hosmer to Mark Vientos. But all have been hitters except for one: right-hander Shaun Anderson, who went on to the University of Florida before emerging as a third-round pick in 2016. Snow hopes to be the first pitcher from the program to be drafted since lefty Brandon Barriera was a first-rounder in '22 and just the fourth arm to be taken from the school since Anderson was a late-round pick who didn’t sign back in '13. Snow is a slightly undersized right-hander who gives off some Sonny Gray vibes in terms of his body type. After missing some time earlier this spring with an oblique issue, he came back throwing extremely well. He’s been up to 97-98 mph as his senior season wore on, showing he can maintain his velocity deep into starts. He backs it up with what he might call two different breaking balls, but is really an effective 78-80 mph power slurve, one with tight three-quarters shape with late finish when he’s landing it well. He has feel for a firm 85-87 mph changeup that can have depth and fade, but he doesn’t throw it much in games. Because of his size and his occasionally spotty command, there are some reliever risk concerns that might cap his Draft stock a bit. Some scouts put his ceiling at around the third round, and it might take him being selected there -- or paid at that level when taken a bit later -- to keep him from following in Anderson’s footsteps to pitch for the Gators in college.

Bishop Verot High School in Fort Myers, Fla., has had a handful of players drafted from its program over the years, but none since 2011, the year the Cubs selected Daniel Vogelbach in the second round. Right-hander Hudson Boyd was actually selected before Vogelbach, and now Knaak has the chance to be the first pitcher from the school to be taken in the Draft after pitching very well at the National High School Invitational and continuing to be a consistent starter all spring. At the NHSI, Knaak shut down California’s Aquinas High School and Draft prospect Eric Bitonti by efficiently mixing all of his pitches well in the strike zone, and it was more of the same all spring. While he’s typically in the 90-93 mph range with his fastball, it has good sink down in the zone, and he maintains his velocity deep into starts. His best pitch is his changeup, an upper-70s offspeed pitch that flashes plus and can fall off the table -- an offering he’ll throw to hitters on both sides of the plate. He’s done a good job landing his mid-70s spike curve for strikes, and he’s incorporated a usable slider as well. A good athlete on the mound, Knaak does a nice job of repeating his delivery and controlling both sides of the plate. He’s not the type of super-projectable prep right-hander you can dream about, but his combination of stuff and ability to maintain it through outings to go along with his feel for the strike zone could have a lot of teams interested in this Clemson recruit.

Harvard-Westlake High School in California can boast alumni arms like Lucas Giolito, Max Fried and Jack Flaherty, but they haven’t had one drafted since Flaherty was a first-round pick by the Cardinals in 2016. That could change this year, and scouts could get a 2-for-1 deal when checking out first-round talent Bryce Rainer at shortstop and Marsten on the mound. The right-hander had Tommy John surgery as a sophomore and missed the 2022 season, but he’d been showing enough stuff, including in front of a lot of evaluators at USA Baseball’s National High School Invitational, this spring to generate early-round buzz. The 6-foot-3 right-hander made a big statement right out of the gate, showing a 95-99 mph heater in his first start while flashing a plus breaking ball and changeup. It backed up a little since then, though he was still consistently up to 94 mph with his heater at the NHSI. When it’s on, his slider is up to 85 mph, and it’s short and tight. Some area scouts think his changeup might be even better, thrown 82-84 mph with excellent depth. He seems to have scrapped a slower curve he’d used in previous seasons, but there’s feel to spin here. Marsten is strong and athletic on the mound with a sound and repeatable delivery that reminds some of Gerrit Cole, pointing to a future of strike-throwing with a north-south arsenal. Some teams may pause because of the injury history or the fact he’ll be 19 at the Draft, but he could be a very exciting Draft-eligible sophomore coming out of Wake Forest’s pitching lab should he head to school.

When most baseball fans think about Notre Dame High School talent in recent years, Hunter Greene (2017) comes to mind, with Giancarlo Stanton ten years earlier. The program hasn’t had a position player taken in the top 10 rounds since 2009, but Madrid hopes to buck that trend this July. The catcher wasn’t seen all that much on the summer showcase circuit but was impressing both area scouts and cross-checkers during his senior year, particularly with his work behind the dish. Madrid’s calling card is his defense. His abilities behind the plate give him a very high floor, with some evaluators claiming he has the best arm of any young catcher they’ve seen this year. It’s not just pure arm strength, as he also has a quick release and is very accurate controlling the running game. His overall defensive package, including receiving and blocking, is quite advanced. His ultimate ceiling will be determined by how much he hits. More than one scout gave a report that included a version of, “if he hits at all, he’s a big leaguer.” The Oregon recruit does have some raw power that he’s gotten to in games at times in front of evaluators, and a team that saw enough of that might look past the typically tough right-right high school catching profile to sign him away from his college commitment.

Morton damaged tendons in his throwing wrist while hitting fungoes as a Minnesota high school senior in 2023, so he made just two starts at the beginning of that season -- and reached 97 mph with his fastball and 91 with his cutter. He turned down a lucrative offer from the Brewers in the 19th around to attend Texas A&M, where he worked just 19 1/3 innings in two years while battling the strike zone and an oblique injury. After transferring back home, he became Minnesota's best pitching prospect since 2020 No. 3 overall pick Max Meyer before blowing out his elbow in his final regular-season start and requiring Tommy John surgery. Morton generates premium stuff from a sidearm slot and low release height, creating plenty of run and sink on a fastball that operates at 93-95 mph and touches 97. He produces premium spin rates on a mid-80s slider with excessive sweep and a cutter that parks in the low 90s. His firm upper-80s changeup features some fade but doesn't fool hitters. While Morton displayed much better control than he did with the Aggies, he caught the heart of the plate too often. None of his offerings elicit many chases because he throws so many strikes, and only his slider qualifies as a swing-and-miss pitch (while his sinker is valuable because it generates so much groundball contact). He doesn't have a weapon to get lefties out, though better command could help.

Because Jasa was so raw when he arrived at Nebraska as a Colorado high school recruit, Cornhuskers coaches not only redshirted him in 2024 but also wouldn't allow him to work against teammates in practice for fear he might injure them with an errant pitch. After posting an 8.68 ERA with 19 walks in 18 2/3 innings in his college debut last year, he has taken a huge step forward in 2026. He emerged as the ace of a team that earned Nebraska's first NCAA regional host bid in 18 years and displayed the best arm in the program since Joba Chamberlain two decades ago. Jasa averages 96 mph and reaches 98 with his fastball, but it lacks life and command and tends to get hit harder than would be expected, so he has used it just 28 percent of the time this spring. He leans much more on a tight upper-80s slider that tops out at 91 and plays well off his best pitch, a downer 78-82 mph curveball. Opponents went 6-for-111 (.054) with 81 strikeouts against his curve in 2026. Though he doesn't employ his low-80s changeup very often and has difficulty landing it for strikes, it shows promising tumble and fade at its best. Jasa has much better feel for his breaking balls than his dead-zone fastball, and while his control has improved, it's still below average. That means he comes with a good deal of reliever risk, though he also has huge upside as a starter if a team can help him improve his ability to shape and locate his heater. He's athletic and has improved tremendously in college, leading to hope he can continue to do so at the next level.

José Veras was a big right-handed pitcher who carved out a nine-year big league career as a reliever for eight different teams after signing out of the Dominican Republic. His equally large son Genson wants to go into the family business, albeit in a different division. Veras has gone to TNXL Academy in Florida for high school and offers some serious offensive upside, though swing-and-miss on the summer showcase circuit really hurt his Draft stock. The younger Veras stands at 6-foot-6, just like his dad, and is a lean and strong 225 pounds. A right-handed hitter and thrower, he possesses the tools of an everyday outfielder if he can get to them consistently. After posting a large strikeout rate over the summer, he made some adjustments during his senior year, both in his approach and in simplifying his swing, helping him get to his huge raw power a bit more consistently while facing a lot of junior college pitching. Veras runs well for his size, clocking solid 60-yard dash times and showing he can steal a base. He’s played center field for TNXL, and a team could send him out there, but he’s probably best suited for right, where his above-average arm would play well. The team deciding to try to sign him away from his Florida State commitment will be the one who felt they saw enough this spring to believe he can make enough contact to get to the impact necessary for an outfield corner at the next level.

Shelar is the latest prospect out of a Marist School (Atlanta) program that has produced seven big leaguers, most notably Kyle Farmer, and won 14 Georgia state championships. He's a physical player with an interesting combination of raw power and solid speed, and a team that believes in his bat could pay him a seven-figure bonus. If that doesn't happen, he'll head to Mississippi State. Already 6-foot-2 and 205 pounds, Shelar projects to have well-above-average raw power thanks to his combination of bat speed, strength and leverage. He led all high schoolers with 19 homers in 33 games this spring. There are mixed opinions about his bat, with some scouts worrying about his ability to make consistent contact against pro pitching. He takes aggressive hacks with an unorthodox right-handed stroke that can get uphill. If he does hit enough to tap into his pop, Shelar has the solid speed to become at least a 20-20 player. A center fielder in high school, he doesn’t have a quick first step but covers ground once he gets going. He likely will wind up on a corner in the long run and has the arm strength and offensive profile to fit in right field.

Gloucester Catholic High School is a powerhouse program in New Jersey, having won four straight state titles and a Garden State-leading 23 overall. But the school hasn’t had a player drafted since 2016, when Tyler Mondile was a sixth-round pick of the Reds. Danza, a strong and toolsy infielder who was named to NJ.com’s first-team All-State squad, could have become the first position player taken from Gloucester since 2009 but withdrew from the Draft and will attend Mississippi State. A 6-foot-2 right-handed hitter, Danza didn’t wow scouts last summer at the East Coast Pro Showcase but had all of his tools on display as the weather warmed in New Jersey during his senior year. He has outstanding bat speed with plenty of strength that generates a ton of raw power. With that comes a good amount of swing-and-miss, though he had stretches of being very locked in this spring. He records plus run times in 60 yard dashes, though that doesn’t always translate to acumen on the basepaths yet. Danza’s plus arm will play on the left side of the infield, but most think he’ll be best suited to shift over from his current shortstop to third, where he can be more of a reactionary defender. Questions about the hit tool at the next level might have made make some pause, but he'll have time to develop his overall toolset with the Bulldogs.

Sandefer’s college passport has been well-stamped in Florida. He began his post-prep career at Division II St. Leo before moving to Central Florida and pitching in a bit of a swing role as a sophomore. He hit the transfer portal again and headed to the University of Florida, presumably for the chance to start. A minor injury had him working out of the pen to start the year and he didn’t look comfortable, though he got in a groove over a couple of mid-week starts to earn a spot in the weekend rotation. That’s been an up-and-down experience, especially in SEC play, and he seemed to dodge a bullet when x-rays came back negative after a comebacker hit him on his pitching arm during the conference tournament. While not the biggest right-hander in the world at 6-foot-1, Sandefer’s stuff could give him the chance to start. He’s seen his fastball tick upwards a bit this year, now sitting over 93 mph and touching 98 mph, and he backs it up with an interesting array of secondary offerings. He can miss bats with his low-80s slider with high spin, a breaker that can be a super-wide sweeper with angle, though it’s inconsistent at times. He sells his low-80s changeup well with his arm speed and it features good fade and depth. He mixes in a cutter at times as well. All of Sandefer’s repertoire comes from a really whippy arm and a low slot, with movement to everything he throws, and he’s generally around the plate. His inconsistencies in conference play might have halted his helium a bit, but a team taking him in the top several rounds could send him out as a starter with the option to shorten him up for a life in the bullpen if that role doesn’t stick.

Sandefer’s college passport has been well-stamped in Florida. He began his post-prep career at Division II St. Leo before moving to Central Florida and pitching in a bit of a swing role as a sophomore. He hit the transfer portal again and headed to the University of Florida, presumably for the chance to start. A minor injury had him working out of the pen to start the year and he didn’t look comfortable, though he got in a groove over a couple of mid-week starts to earn a spot in the weekend rotation. That’s been an up-and-down experience, especially in SEC play, and he seemed to dodge a bullet when x-rays came back negative after a comebacker hit him on his pitching arm during the conference tournament. From the minute he arrived on campus, Hansen has been a member of the UC Irvine weekend rotation, making 16 starts as a freshman and 16 more as a sophomore in 2025 en route to earning First-Team All Big West honors. He was the Anteaters’ Friday night starter once again this season, with mixed results, but his consistency and durability have him in position to join Andre Pallante (2019 fourth round) and Riley Kelly (2025 fourth round) as Irvine pitchers taken recently in the top several rounds. With a strong 6-foot-2 frame, there's nothing glamorous about how Hansen gets things done on the mound, but he has a legitimate three-pitch mix with an idea of how to use it and the ability to routinely go deep into starts. His fastball is generally in the 90-95 mph range, though he was showing a tick more velocity this year sitting 93-94. He commands it well and has shown he can get to more later in games, giving some hope there could be more consistent mph to come. He has an above-average 81-84 mph curve, and his 84-85 mph changeup flashes plus; combined, the two secondary offerings missed bats at a 39-percent clip in 2026. Hansen is around the zone with all of his offerings, but while his compact arm action adds deception, hiding the ball well, some scouts don’t love his below-average extension. There is strong consensus that he has plus makeup and a nasty competitive streak, which could give him the chance to start long-term, albeit with a more limited ceiling.

Yehl was an effective part of West Virginia’s bullpen right out of the gate as a freshman in 2023, then did it again in 2024 following a solid turn in the Cape Cod League. Scouts had to wait to see what kind of progress he might have made as a junior because Tommy John surgery knocked out the 2025 season. He returned in 2026 and slotted into the weekend rotation in his first chance to start, finishing the year as the Friday night starter, earning Big 12 Pitcher of the Year honors and winning the Mountaineers’ Super Regional clincher that launched them to the College World Series for the first time. While he only has this season as a starter on his resume, Yehl’s size and pure stuff should at least give him a chance to stick in a rotation at the next level. The 6-foot-6 lefty has shown the ability to get his fastball up to 96-97 mph, especially early in the season. As the Mountaineers were preparing for Omaha, Yehl showed some signs of fatigue and a loss of a tick or two of velocity, but that's understandable given he’s just a year removed from elbow surgery, and he’s well beyond any innings total previously accumulated in his career. Yehl’s best secondary pitch is his slider, which flashes above average and has been up to 87 mph and more around 83-84 mph late. At times he’ll show signs of a distinct cutter and curve, but they do run into each other a bit. He has an upper-80s changeup that doesn’t get called much but could be solid with pro development. Even when fatigued, the 22-year-old Yehl has shown improved strike-throwing and is a plus competitor. If starting doesn’t work out, his fastball-slider combination should work out of a bullpen.

Part of a Blair Oaks (Wardsville, Mo.) program that spawned Tom Henke, Libbert impressed on the showcase circuit last summer and consistently displayed quality stuff as a senior. He climbed Draft boards all spring and looked headed for the top three rounds despite his commitment to Missouri. He struck out 18 in six innings during his final start in early May, but he injured his elbow and required Tommy John surgery. Libbert regularly works with a low-90s fastball that reaches 97 mph and plays better than its velocity because of its significant carry up in the zone. He has precocious feel for a low-80s changeup that can be a plus pitch at its best. He also has aptitude for spinning the ball, though his upper-70s curveball and slider with similar velocity can blend together at times. Libbert's 6-foot-1, 205-pound frame is more strong than projectable, but he already has the makings of three solid or better offerings. Though there's some effort in his delivery, it's also deceptive and doesn't prevent him from throwing strikes. He repeats his mechanics well and stands out with his competitiveness.

There hasn’t been a high school catcher from Oregon drafted since some guy named Adley Rutschman went in the 40th round in 2016 before heading to Oregon State. Only three prep backstops have signed and made it to the big leagues in Draft history, led by Dale Murphy, who made most of his big league noise as an outfielder. Scott could follow in Rutschman’s footsteps by playing for the Beavers in college, though he did attend the MLB Draft Combine to show off his skills to all 30 teams. Strong and compact, Scott is a sub-six foot right-handed-hitting catcher with some skills on both sides of the ball. He makes consistent hard contact and has feel for the barrel, particularly for a guy who is more strength than bat speed with an air-driven swing that generates solid raw power. He runs well, with some scouts getting above-average run times to first base, and is a terrific athlete who played point guard for his high school basketball team and is graduating as that team’s all-time leading scorer. Some scouts have seen a plus arm from Scott, and he combines it with a good setup and decent hands behind the dish. He also has a strong desire to stay behind the plate, which is needed for a player to catch long-term. There’s not a ton of projection, and the right-right high school catching profile is a rough one for teams to buy into, but some could be interested in keeping his all-around skillset from heading to Corvallis in the fall.

Torrey Pines High School in Southern California has had a dozen players get drafted over the years, with four eventually touching the big leagues. Two of them have been there this year in Carson Williams and Kyle Hurt. Jutronich has the chance to be the first left-handed pitcher ever selected from the school, and his combination of ceiling and athleticism had scouts touting him as a potential top-three-round pick, though missing two months of his senior season with an arm issue has halted his momentum. At 6-foot-4, 190 pounds, Jutronich screams projection from the left side. His fastball is below-average right now -- he’ll pitch at 89-90 mph, topping out at 92-93 -- but there’s strong conviction there will be more velocity to come when he adds strength to his frame. He has good feel to spin, with a slider that’s a bit ahead of his slower curve. He also exhibits feel for a changeup. Jutronich’s athleticism adds to an ease of operation on the mound, and he tends to be a reliable strike-thrower. He did make it back for two outings post-injury, with mixed results, but it helped assuage any health-related fears teams might have had. He’s committed to go to UC Santa Barbara, which has a very good reputation for developing pitching -- think Shane Bieber, Michael McGreevy, last year’s No. 2 pick Tyler Bremner or this year’s top pitching prospect, Jackson Flora -- so seeing Jutronich emerge in three years as a first-rounder might be in the back of some evaluators’ minds.

Part of a deeper than usual New York prep pitching crop in 2023 that also included Brewers supplemental first-rounder Josh Knoth and future North Carolina ace Jason DeCaro, LeGuernic deflected interest from pro clubs to attend Clemson. He logged an 8.62 ERA in his first two years with the Tigers before cutting that mark to 4.69 as a full-time reliever as a junior. Scouts believe he has a lot of untapped potential, so he could go a few rounds earlier than his performance might indicate. LeGuernic owns one of the more unhittable sliders in the college class, a mid-80s breaker with high spin rates and huge sweeping action. His fastball operates in the mid 90s and touches 98 mph with carry and armside run, though right-handers crush it more than they should. Both pitches added 3-4 mph this spring. He doesn't have much faith in an upper-80s changeup with mild fade that he can't land in the zone often enough to tempt hitters. Working from an extremely low arm slot gives LeGuernic deception as well as sweep on his slider, though it also hampers his control and command. His quick arm and 6-foot-4 frame have some scouts wondering if he could succeed as a starter in pro ball, though he'd need to do a better job of locating his pitches and refine his changeup. It's more realistic to project him as a slider-happy reliever who can carve up left-handers.

Nevada's best prep pitching prospect in 2023, Mercurius spent his first two college seasons at Nevada-Las Vegas before transferring to Oklahoma to reunite with his brother Xander, the Silver State's top high school arm in 2025. L.J. can look like a second-round talent at his best and opened this spring by allowing one earned run in four non-conference starts before pitching his way out of the rotation by mid-May. He played a key bullpen role for the Sooners and won the clinching game at the College World Series. Mercurius operates with a 92-94 mph fastball that peaks at 97 with improved carry but not much running action, so it gets in trouble when he doesn't locate it well. The same is true with his mid-80s changeup, a plus offering with fade and sink that was victimized for five homers in his first seven SEC starts. He relies primarily on those two pitches while mixing in some tight low-80s sliders. The Sooners have raised Mercurius' arm slot to get more backspin on his fastball, similar to what they did with first-rounder Kyson Witherspoon in 2025. He's throwing more strikes as a junior than he did last year but his ability to improve his command will determine his future success. If he can't, he'll be more middle reliever than No. 4 starter.

The Oregon high school baseball scene has produced some serious early-round talent in recent years, though most of it has come on the mound, with first-rounders like Mick Abel, Noble Meyer and Kruz Schoolcraft. The 2026 prep class in the Beaver State is a bit thinner, but there are some interesting hitters to consider in the top several rounds. Nelson is among the best of the group, a name that was moving up boards the more scouts saw him this spring, giving him the chance to be just the second Oregonian high school hitter, joining 2025 draftee Slater de Brun, to go in the top five rounds since 2012. Nelson is a left-handed-hitting shortstop who you might have to see more than once to fully appreciate. He has some feel for the barrel, with some looseness to his swing and some bat speed, to go along with solid pitch recognition. He lacks impact right now, with a tendency to have too much pull-side roll over contact. There’s a little juice to that side and given his clean bat path and ability to carry the barrel through the zone, there’s some hope that there will be some power to come as he fills out his frame. A plus runner, Nelson is an aggressive baserunner who can steal bags. His athleticism plays on the dirt as well, and he couples it with a good game clock and instincts to give him the chance to play shortstop for a long time, with more than enough arm for the premium position. He’s committed to Loyola Marymount for college ball.

Lujo won four Florida state 7-A titles and three national championships in four seasons at Stoneman Douglas HS (Parkland, Fla.). After batting .361 as a freshman at Dayton in 2025, he transferred to Georgia and became one of the best hitters in the Southeastern Conference, posting a .394 average in league play as the Bulldogs won the regular-season and tournament crowns. He's the grandson of Rennie Stennett, who won two World Series rings with the Pirates and is the only modern big leaguer to collect seven hits in a nine-inning game. A right-handed hitter, Lujo has quality bat-to-ball skills and a patient approach. He rarely ventures out of the strike zone and makes repeated line-drive contact against all types of offerings, though he doesn't walk very often. He tends to work fastballs from gap to gap and turn on secondary pitches, and he could enhance his 12-15 homer power if he learns to launch more balls in the air. Lujo uses his plus speed to beat out infield hits and steal bases. A third baseman at Dayton, he has the hands and feet to play the middle infield but throwing issues prevented him from claiming that role at Georgia. He shifted to center field, where he's still honing his instincts but could develop into an average to solid defender with fringy arm strength.

Wright starred in two seasons at Bowling Green State, winning Mid-American Conference Freshman of the Year honors in 2024 and Defensive Player of the Year accolades in 2025. He also led the MAC with a .503 on-base percentage in his first season and with a .406 batting average and .513 OBP before transferring to Tennessee. Though a broken hamate in his left hand required surgery and cost him the first three weeks of the season, he has been the Volunteers' best hitter this season and is one of the more athletic catchers available. Wright combines bat-to-ball skills with an extremely aggressive approach, chasing a ton of pitches yet making a lot of line-drive contact and rarely missing fastballs. The right-handed hitter slugged just .243 with wood bats in the Cape Cod League last summer and doesn't do a lot of damage against premium velocity, so he may not have more than 10-15 homer power. While his swing-at-everything mindset cuts into his walk totals, he enhances his on-base ability by getting hit by an excessive amount of pitches. Unlike most catchers, Wright can flash plus speed and is capable of playing center field. He has spent more time in center than behind the plate this year while recovering from his hamate injury but offers more value as a backstop. He's an effective receiver and blocker with solid arm strength.

In 2020, Jacob Berry was a solid high school prospect in Arizona who went on to spend two years in college -- one at Arizona and one at Louisiana State -- en route to being a first-round pick of the Marlins in '22. Now it’s his younger brother Jet’s turn to follow in the family business -- dad, Perry, played pro ball and sister Jade is an infielder on Stanford’s softball team -- as one of the more talented high school hitters in the Four Corners. Like his brother, Jet is a switch-hitter with abilities from both sides, though that’s where the sibling similarities end. The younger Berry is smaller, twitchy and athletic, and while he does have a chance for a little impact from both sides of the plate, he’s more of a hit-over-power kind of guy. His best tool is his easily plus speed, sometimes recording 70 run times, making him a constant threat on the basepaths. Aside from future offensive impact, the other main question around Berry is where he’ll play at the next level. Some scouts won’t rule out his ability to play shortstop, with decent hands and actions, but some feel his arm is short for the left side of the infield. He could be an average defender at second base or center field, though teams might have to wait for two years when he’ll be a Draft-eligible sophomore at Arizona State.

Scolari was playing his high school ball in Reno, Nev., when Tommy John surgery knocked out his senior year. He spent his true freshman year at San Diego rehabbing from the injury and didn’t throw a competitive pitch. Now a Draft-eligible redshirt freshman, Scolari settled in as the Toreros’ Friday night starter in 2025, showing off some arm strength and projection while earning West Coast Conference Pitcher of the Year honors, though his long-term role remains in question. Scolari has added some size and strength to his frame and now stands at 6-foot-4 and 200 pounds. He mostly relies on his fastball and slider combination to get outs. His fastball is up to 96 mph, typically sitting 92-93, but he misses a fair amount of bats with the lively heater. His low-80s slider can be an out pitch, but it’s inconsistent. He does have some developing feel for an upper-80s changeup, though it’s behind the other two offerings. While he has a starting pitcher’s frame and solid delivery, Scolari’s fringy command -- to go along with his lack of a dependable third pitch -- does lead to some starter vs. reliever questions. There also is a bit of a lack of track record here given that the first pitch he threw this season was the first he’d thrown since his junior year of high school, but that also means there could be some intriguing upside potential to reach.

Scolari was playing his high school ball in Reno, Nev., when Tommy John surgery knocked out his senior year. He spent his true freshman year at San Diego rehabbing from the injury and didn’t throw a competitive pitch. Now a Draft-eligible redshirt freshman, Scolari settled in as the Toreros’ Friday night starter in 2025, showing off some arm strength and projection while earning West Coast Conference Pitcher of the Year honors, though his long-term role remains in question. The high school baseball scene in and around Jacksonville, Florida, has produced some serious Draft prospects. Chipper Jones leads that list, obviously, and Javier Báez is the last first-rounder from the area. More recently, Aaron Watson was a prep right-handed pitcher to get an over-slot deal last year in the second round. Dennis won’t go as early as Watson, but he does represent the best high school arm in the area as a bit of a pop-up player who hadn’t done much on the showcase circuit last summer but was garnering interest as a converted catcher and two-way guy with upside on the mound that was on display all spring and at the MLB Draft Combine. It’s Dennis’ size and arm strength that stand out more than anything currently. The 6-foot-4 right-hander has plenty of present velocity, throwing his fastball up to 96 mph, and he was sitting 95-96 mph during his Combine outing. It can occasionally feature some arm side run, though it also can straighten out too frequently. He backs it up with an 83-85 mph slider with excellent vertical break that has the chance to be a plus pitch in the future. His changeup is his third pitch, but he did mix in a few upper-80s low-spin cambios at the Combine. Strong and fairly athletic, Dennis comes at hitters with a simplified stretch-only delivery and does a decent job of being around the zone, though he’s definitely control over command as more of a thrower than pitcher presently. His 12 homers as a senior was among the best of any Florida prep hitter, but his future is on the mound, even though some evaluators seeing a future reliever, whether it’s in pro ball or at Jacksonville University.

TNXL Academy in Florida has a trio of Draft prospects who could all go in the top several rounds. Genson Veras is the bat scouts like, while evaluators can pick between a pair of different arms in Coleton Brady and Spencer Evans. While Brady’s feel for pitching is better, Evans has showcased better pure stuff from the left side, starting at summer showcase events like East Coast Pro Showcase and USA Baseball’s 18U National Team Camp and continuing into this year, albeit with less strikes overall. Evans offers a combination of size (6-foot-3), projection and arm strength. Combine that with the fact that he's left-handed, and that’s sure to intrigue teams. At times, he can look like a first-round caliber talent, with a fastball routinely up to 95-96 mph and flashing two above-average secondary offerings. He’s added velocity to what is now a low-80s slider and can miss a lot of bats with it, throwing the breaker with good angles. His mid-80s changeup continues to improve. As good as that package sounds, Evans is often stuff over performance, with his command and control the biggest culprit in keeping him ineffective. He’s prone to walks and comes with a little left-handed reliever risk, but he’s athletic and moves easily on the mound. A team that sees enough future starter in him could try to sign him away from his commitment to Louisiana State.

A solid prospect as a projectable right-hander in the California high school ranks, Segura went undrafted in 2023 because of his strong commitment to Oregon State. He made an immediate impact on campus, serving in the Beavers’ weekend rotation as a freshman, then spent most of his sophomore year pitching out of the bullpen with mixed results. Given another chance to stick in Oregon State’s weekend rotation as a junior, Segura ran with the opportunity, finishing in the top 10 among Division I pitchers with a 2.22 ERA, finishing off his season with a 10-strikeout Regional win as an exclamation point. When the 2026 season began, most scouts would have pegged Segura for a sure-thing reliever role in the future. But his stuff -- and his feel for how to mix it -- improved, with three legitimate offerings that now have some evaluators thinking he can start. His fastball sits around 94 mph and is up to 96, and while it’s not a huge swing-and-miss pitch, it does get some chase and it’s sink leads to a lot of groundballs (62 percent GB rate in '26, per Synergy). The big separator has been how his slider has taken a leap forward. It’s a low-80s breaker that missed bats as he got on top of it more consistently than in the past for better angle and tilt. His upper-80s changeup is his third pitch, but he has good feel for it, especially against left-handed hitters. After walking nearly six per nine as a sophomore, Segura’s strike-throwing was vastly improved this season (3.3 BB/9) and he took the ball every weekend. That could give more confidence to a team taking him on Day 2 and at least present him the opportunity to start at the outset of his pro career.

Every year there are players who take a large step forward in their Draft season, pop-up prospects as they’re generally known. Barker has been one of those players in the Four Corners. After not being seen much on the summer showcase circuit, Barker started showing off his raw tools as his Casteel High School made it to USA Baseball’s National High School Invitational semifinals, and that continued this spring as Casteel advanced to the second round of the Arizona state playoffs. Barker is a super-athletic left-handed hitter who plays the infield in high school. Everything about him is a little raw, but there are glimpses of him doing everything well. It’s a hit-over-power approach, and those who like him see an average hit tool in there, though he’ll have to continue to add strength to his 6-foot-1 frame to get to more impact, even if he’s never a huge power guy. The one purely plus tool he has is his speed, and some scouts have seen 70-grade run times from him occasionally. Where Barker best profiles defensively is also a question. He has some abilities to play short but had been seeing most of his time on the dirt at third base this spring. His bat might not profile well for the corner infield spot, and his overall defense needs work, with some thinking he might fit in a 3B/2B/LF kind of role. Those who like him are all about projection, but some think he’d be better off going to Texas Tech, where he’d be a Draft-eligible sophomore in two years.

High school players in the northeast are often late risers simply because it takes a while for the weather to warm up and for them to get going. Add in a winter sport like basketball to delay being seen as another reason for a player to be a bit of a pop-up guy. And when that player didn’t play on the summer showcase circuit, they can really seem like they come out of nowhere. Plunkett checks off all three boxes, but the New York prepster’s name was coming up more frequently in scout chatter as the season moved closer to the Draft. An athletic 6-foot-3, Plunkett certainly looks the part. The right-handed hitter has a smooth swing that is currently line-drive oriented, but it’s easy to project plenty more raw power to come because his frame should be able to add plenty of strength as he matures. He’ll show it off in batting practice at times, but there’s not that much impact in games to date. Plunkett’s athleticism also helps him defensively. He looks like he could stick at shortstop for a while, with enough arm and more to come, good actions and solid instincts. He might look like a collection of 50 grades, but that’s a solid big leaguer, and there could be a lot more in the tank. He’s committed to Binghamton for college, but there’s been some buzz that he could be like a Matthew Ferrara type, who was an over-slot ninth-round signing by the Phillies in 2025, or even Michael Oliveto, a surprise supplemental first-round pick by the Tigers last year.

A two-way star in high school whose future is on the mound, Willoughby scored the game-winning run in extra innings in the Kentucky state championship game last June before performing well on the showcase circuit. Gatorade's 2026 Kentucky prep player of the year, he won another state title by spinning a one-hit shutout in the finale. A Kentucky commit, he'd be eligible for the Draft as a 21-year-old sophomore in 2028. Willoughby's fastball sits at 93-95 mph and tops out at 97 with armside run in short stints, though he works more in the low 90s when he ventures deeper into games. He displays advanced feel for a mid-80s changeup with fade and sink, and his cambio could become a plus pitch. He trusts it more than an upper-70s slider that features promising sweep but needs more power. Willoughby has a clean three-quarters delivery that translates into strikes with all three of his offerings. He already can spot his fastball to both sides of the plate and should add more velocity as he fills out his 6-foot-2 frame. He might blossom into a mid-rotation starter if he can refine a harder, more reliable slider.

Gallaher has established himself as one of the most clutch playoff performers in college baseball, earning MVP honors at NCAA regionals in each of his first two seasons while leading North Carolina to the Men's College World Series in 2024 and a victory shy of a return last June. Though he was the Tar Heels' best hitter as a sophomore, he hasn't performed as well this spring and scouts aren't quite sure what to make of him. He has slugged just .316 with two homers in 52 games during two summers with wood bats in the Cape Cod League, which hurts his cause. A right-handed hitter, Gallaher doesn't have any obvious weaknesses at the plate. He manages the strike zone well enough, shows the ability to handle lefties and righties and all types of pitches and makes hard flyball contact from gap to gap. His lack of power with wood is a concern, especially with a player who may not be able to handle a challenging defensive position. A below-average runner with average arm strength, Gallaher manned third base in his first two college seasons but the game sped up on him too much there. UNC shifted him to second base this year and he has played better than scouts expected. Some still question whether he has the actions and quickness to man the keystone in pro ball, so he could wind up in left field.

Scouts have been trying to figure out Vigue since his days as Massachusetts high schooler, when he could be unhittable at times and unable to find the strike zone at others. That pattern continued in two years at Michigan, where he went undrafted as a sophomore-eligible in 2025. After switching schools, he has had an up-and-down season as Georgia's No. 2 starter and missed a turn in the rotation in late April with forearm tightness. Vigue gets more horizontal separation between his fastball and slider than almost any pitcher in the college crop. His 93-95 mph sinker reaches 98 with significant armside run, while his mid-80s slider has huge sweep in the opposite direction. He has utilized those two offerings 95 percent of the time this spring, rarely using a low-90s cutter and upper-80s changeup. Vigue generates plenty of swings and misses with his slider and weak contact with his fastball, but he has great difficulty landing either pitch in the zone on a regular basis. He rarely works past five innings, running up high pitch counts when hitters lay off his slider or he can't command his sinker. He has a strong 6-foot-3, 230-pound frame and a delivery that should provide more strikes, giving hope that he can add a third pitch and succeed as a starter in pro ball, but realistically he's more of a reliever.

Jorvorskie Lane Sr. rushed for a Texas A&M-record 49 touchdowns before spending three seasons in the National Football League. His son punishes baseballs rather than linebackers and is one of the more intriguing athletes and youngest players in the 2026 prep class. He projected as a first-round pick and drew Andrew McCutchen comps earlier in his high school career, though struggles during the summer and his senior season have dropped his stock. Lane has the potential for four solid-or-better tools but the key to his success will be the fifth. He creates impressive bat speed and raw power but his right-handed swing gets too long and uphill. He has difficulty making contact against quality pitching and does little damage when he doing so. Lane features plus speed and some evaluators give him the same grades for his arm and center-field play. There are some mixed reviews about his defense and thoughts that the Arkansas recruit may wind up on an outfield corner. He has also seen time at catcher and in the middle infield.

Conover was Cowley County (Kan.) CC's top hitter as a freshman in 2024, slashing .378/.508/.684, but his tendency to chase pitches limited him to part-time play last spring after he transferred to Oklahoma State. He toned down his approach as a junior and boosted his OPS from .843 to 1.101. He doesn't have a standout tool but also lacks a glaring weakness, and scouts love his makeup. Conover has a quick left-handed stroke but is content to work the middle of the field and drives more balls to left field with authority than he does to his pull side. He cut his chase rate from 26 percent in 2025 to 19 percent this spring, which made a huge difference because he rarely swings and misses against strikes, especially versus fastballs. The next adjustment will be to curb his tendency to make ground-ball contact, which cuts into what should be at least average power. Enhancing average speed with good instincts on the bases, Conover will pick his spots to steal and take extra bags. Primarily a left fielder for the Cowboys, he's an average defender with arm strength to match. He caught in high school and during fall practice, and the idea of moving him behind the plate intrigues some clubs.

Scouts liked Voegele's arsenal and athleticism when he was an Illinois high schooler, and the Diamondbacks took a 20th-round flier on him in 2023 before he headed to Kansas. He quickly became the Jayhawks' No. 2 starter and won Big 12 Conference Freshman of the Year accolades in 2024, then pitched for the U.S. collegiate national team that summer. He didn't enjoy as much success as Kansas' Friday-night guy for much of the last two years, logging a 5.77 ERA, though he did set a school record with 120 strikeouts in 97 innings this spring. While Voegele works with a 93-96 mph fastball and can push it to 98, it lacks life, and he too often leaves it over the middle of the plate, so it can get pounded. When he can get ahead in the count with his heater, he can put hitters away with a low-80s curveball with downer break and a tighter, harder slider. He never has exhibited much feel for a changeup, and his upper-80s cambio is more of a batting-practice fastball. Voegele is athletic and provides consistent strikes, but his delivery lacks extension and deception. He maintains his velocity deep into games but has to improve the action and command with his fastball. He'll need to make some adjustments to remain a starter rather than becoming a breaking ball-heavy reliever at the next level.

Gomez-Gudiño and his family fled Venezuela three years ago, enduring a harrowing journey on foot, by bus and by boat -- including some near-death experiences -- to get to the United States. They eventually made it to Arizona and he found a baseball home at Saguaro HS in Scottsdale. He first jumped on the radar as a sophomore as he showed the ability to handle catching eventual first-round pick Cam Caminiti and continued to make a name for himself last summer at events like Perfect Game National and the Area Code Games. A strong senior season and invite to the nearby MLB Draft Combine this year only enhanced his profile. Offering skills on both sides of the ball, Gomez-Gudiño is a strong switch-hitting 6-foot-1 backstop. He has at least above-average raw power from both sides of the plate, and one of the reasons for his ascension on Draft boards this spring has been his improved feel to hit, with better plate discipline and barrel control. One thing scouts look for in a young catcher is the “want to,” and Gomez-Gudiño clearly loves the position. He has plus raw arm strength, though he needs to refine his accuracy to maximize his effectiveness in controlling the running game. He can occasionally cheat out of his crouch to get throws off, which impacts his ability to block, but all the ingredients are there to make him a potential all-around player at a premium position, leading to many teams considering trying to sign him away from his commitment to South Carolina.

Offering skills on both sides of the ball, Gomez-Gudiño is a strong switch-hitting 6-foot-1 backstop. He has at least above-average raw power from both sides of the plate, and one of the reasons for his ascension on Draft boards this spring has been his improved feel to hit, with better plate discipline and barrel control. One thing scouts look for in a young catcher is the “want to,” and Gomez-Gudiño clearly loves the position. He has plus raw arm strength, though he needs to refine his accuracy to maximize his effectiveness in controlling the running game. He can occasionally cheat out of his crouch to get throws off, which impacts his ability to block, but all the ingredients are there to make him a potential all-around player at a premium position, leading to many teams considering trying to sign him away from his commitment to South Carolina.

While it can be challenging to see and evaluate players from eastern Canada, Omidi has been a bit of a fixture in showcases, from things like the East Coast Pro Showcase and Area Code Games to playing the last two years for the Canadian Junior National Team against professional competition in Minor League Spring Training and in the Dominican Republic. Hailing from the same Ontario high school that produced one-time big leaguer Jordan Balazovic, Omidi has shown some potential, particularly with the bat, while also raising some overall questions about his profile. With a boxy, 6-foot-1 build, Omidi has shown off some strength from the left side of the plate. There have been times where excellent contact skills have been on display, but some swing-and-miss concerns did pop up against some of the better Minor League arms he faced with Team Canada. There is definite raw pop for him to tap into, with strong hands and wrists, and he’ll show off lofty power in batting practice. Omidi is an average runner, though speed isn’t a big part of his game, and he has an average arm, but where he fits defensively long-term is an unanswered question. It’s unlikely he’ll be a shortstop at the next level, lacking the quick first step or range to play there, with some scouts thinking he can handle second and others believing third, which he’s played a lot more of lately, is his best chance to stay on the dirt, with a corner outfield spot a possibility if the infield isn't working. Omidi loves to hit, and it will be his bat that teams will be interested in signing away from his commitment to Kentucky.

Born in Panama City, Guevara was Panama's top hitter at the 18-and-under World Cup in 2022 before his senior season at Georgia Premier Academy (Statesboro). Knee injuries limited him in his first two seasons at Auburn, but he was one of the best all-around players in the Southeastern Conference this spring. He batted .322/.399/.533 with 13 homers and earned SEC all-defensive honors at third base for the second straight year. Though Guevara has been productive with metal bats and generates good exit velocities, there are some questions about how he'll perform at the next level with wood. The right-handed hitter almost never turns on pitches, produces little power against quality fastballs and makes inconsistent contact against breaking balls and changeups. He has an aggressive approach and mainly concentrates on drilling line drives from gap to gap. An average runner, Guevara plays quicker than that at the hot corner. He's an agile defender with solid to plus arm strength, and he got the job done when he opened this season at shortstop. He also has seen action at second base and left field during his college career.

Valley HS (West Des Moines, Iowa) has produced a single big leaguer (Dan Jennings) and has had four players drafted, none higher than the 36th round. Stedman, the Tigers' latest star, could go much higher than that this spring if he's signable away from an Iowa commitment. He performed well at the Area Code Games and World Wood Bat Association World Championship on the showcase circuit and has boosted his velocity as a senior. At his best this spring, Stedman has operated with a 93-95 mph fastball and touched 97 with good carry, though he has setted at 91-95 on other occasions. Scouts are trying to figure out exactly what to make of his low-80s curveball, which features good shape but comes with low spin rates. He shows advanced feel for a fading changeup in the low 80s and also messes around with a cutter in the upper 80s. Stedman impresses with the athleticism and ease in his delivery, and he has no problem providing regular strikes. He has plenty of projection remaining in his 6-foot-3 frame, so he should continue to add power to his pitches. He's far from a finished product but has the potential to become a mid-rotation starter.

With the makings of three solid offerings and the ability to throw strikes, Grant can lead scouts who believe in him the most to dream of him becoming Sonny Gray. But he also lacks projectability, throws with some effort and turned 19 in march, so other evaluators see him as more of a reliever. If he doesn't sign this summer, he'll be Draft-eligible in 2028 after two seasons at Tennessee. Gatorade's Iowa high school player of the year, Grant works at 92-94 mph and reaches 96 with some carry on his fastball. His best offering is a low-80s slider with high spin rates and significant sweep, and he shows the ability to land it for strikes as well as to use it for chases. He also displays some aptitude for a low-80s changeup with fade and sink. Grant can deliver all three of his pitches for strikes and relentlessly challenge hitters. Scouts love his competitiveness, and he tried to pitch with a nasty toe injury in his opening outing this spring before just taking just one week off. His athleticism helps his chances of remaining a starter, though his stuff probably won't get much better than it is now.

After going undrafted as a Nevada high schooler and then in two seasons at Mesa (Ariz.) CC and his first at McNeese State, Nachtsheim has emerged as one of the best college senior prospects in 2026. Though the Cowboys bounced him between closing and starting depending on team need this spring, he set a school record with 129 strikeouts in 93 innings and led NCAA Division I with 98 K's via the heater. McNeese State's best pitching prospect since 2005 first-rounder Jacob Marceaux, Nachtsheim finished the season by allowing just eight runs in five starts. Nachtsheim's fastball parks at 92-94 mph and peaks at 97 while featuring some of the best carry in the Draft, as well as some natural cutting action. He throws his heater three-quarters of the time, utilizing a lackluster low-80s slider as his main secondary option. His fading low-80s changeup works as a chase pitch, but he has trouble landing it in the zone and it often gets hammered when he does. Scouts don't love Nachtsheim's less-than-smooth delivery and arm action, though they don't prevent him from filling the strike zone. He does create quality extension that adds to the deception with his fastball. While he'll likely get the chance to show what he can do as a starter in pro ball, his long-term future almost certainly is as a reliever.

Though he's a 6-foot right-hander who averages 92 mph with his fastball, Harpster should become the third-highest drafted pitcher ever out of East Tennessee State. He won't go as high as 1979 first-rounder Atlee Hammaker or 2020 second-rounder Landon Knack, but his metrics and ability to miss bats with his fastball and cutter are attractive to teams. A fixture in the Buccaneers rotation since early in his freshman season, he generated some of the best fastball and breaking ball spin rates at the MLB Draft Combine. Harpster's heater tops out at 95 mph but plays well above its velocity thanks to its flat approach angle and carry. His mid-80s cutter works better than its radar-gun readings as well because he excels at locating it where hitters will chase it but will be unable to barrel it. He also can shape a low-80s slider with more sweeping action, while his upper-80s changeup features some fade and sink but lags behind the rest of his repertoire. Harpster slings the ball and creates premium deception with an extremely low release point and good extension in his delivery. While his walk rate jumped from 6 percent as a sophomore to 11 percent this spring, he still showed advanced feel for working on the edges of the strike zone. If a pro team can help him add some velocity, he'll become even more intriguing.

Taylor immediately claimed a spot in Cincinnati's weekend rotation as a freshman in 2024 and never relinquished it. He has earned all-Big 12 Conference recognition in each of his three seasons while setting school records for career wins (22) and strikeouts (276), and single-season K's (115 this spring). The Bearcats haven't had a pitcher drafted earlier than the seventh round since third-rounder Dave Sala 40 years ago, but Taylor should end that drought. Taylor consistently brings at least a plus slider to the mound, dealing in the mid 80s with plenty of vertical and horizontal action. He ranked second in NCAA Division I with 80 strikeouts via the slide piece this spring. Cincinnati called for his slider more than his fastball, which usually ranges from 92-94 mph and reaches 97 but lacks life. He barely uses an upper-80s changeup that's too firm and has occasional fade. While Taylor throws with some effort, he has improved his control throughout his college career. He's a durable 6-foot-5, 230-pound workhorse and competes well. He'll need to develop more action on his fastball and refine his changeup to make it as a starter in pro ball, though his slider could make him a late-inning weapon as a reliever.

Govel came for his official visit to Southern Cal four years ago and immediately formed a bond with Mason Edwards. It took a little time for that to translate to the field, especially since Govel redshirted his freshman year in 2024 following Tommy John surgery. But after scuffling through a 2025 season spent mostly in the Trojans’ bullpen, he joined Edwards in the USC weekend rotation to form one of the best 1-2 punches in college baseball. Govel earned NCBWA Second-team All-American honors after finishing fourth among all Division I pitchers with an 0.90 WHIP and topping the Big 10 with his 6.19 K/BB ratio. A strong 6-foot, 200-pound right-hander, Govel might attack hitters with as many as six pitches. He has both a four-seam and newer two-seam fastball that typically sit around 91-92 mph, though he has topped out at 95. He has consistently shown consistent 94-95 mph heaters early in the spring, with 20-21 inches of induced vertical break on the four-seamer. His best secondary offering is a plus low-80s changeup he sells extremely well with arm speed that kills spin and has excellent depth at the plate, a cambio he’ll throw to hitters on both sides. He has both a low-80s slider and an upper-70s bigger top-down curve, and a cutter that flashes average that he can get up to 90 mph. Govel delivers all of his offerings with a quick arm and a simple and repeatable stretch-only delivery. That leads to very good fastball command and excellent overall control that limits walks. His ceiling might be a bit limited, but his repertoire and feel to pitch could help him get to the big leagues as a back-end starter.

Randall was a standout at Northern California high school power De La Salle (a program known for producing lefty Kyle Harrison), but he pulled his name out of the 2023 Draft because he was intent on attending UCLA. After pitching infrequently as a freshman, Randall has been a mainstay in the Bruins’ bullpen. Though he’s never closed, he’s shown his power stuff can dominate top college hitters, leading him to an eye-popping 16.5 K/9 rate and .142 batting average against in his junior year. A 6-foot-4 right-hander, Randall is all about his fastball. To say he’s heater-heavy would be a huge understatement as he threw the pitch -- averaging close to 97 mph and touching triple digits -- 89 percent of the time this spring. It is an extremely effective pitch, but not just because of the velocity. It elicited a 36 percent miss rate this season thanks to a combination of low release and extension to create upshoot arm side life. He basically throws one secondary pitch, an 89-92 mph slider-cutter hybrid that can be effective because it’s hard, but it’s also short and some think he’ll need to come up with something that features more depth at the next level. The other challenge Randall faces is his ability to throw strikes, as he walked 5.4 per nine over his college career at UCLA. He won’t need pinpoint command to be a big league reliever, but a team taking him will hope he can find a little better feel for the zone and add shape to his secondary offering in order to grow into a high-leverage role.

Rhudy throws a lot of fastballs and he throws a lot of strikes. That approach worked for two seasons at Kennesaw State and continued to bring him success in the Southeastern Conference, college baseball's best league, after he transferred to Tennessee for his junior season. He compiled a 3.38 ERA and 41/6 K/BB ratio in 32 innings while ranking among the NCAA Division I leaders in fastball rates of chases (41 percent), swings and misses (35 percent) and in-zone swings and misses (28 percent). Rhudy's heater sits at 91-93 mph and reaches 96, but hitters can't lay off it or catch up to it despite its below-average velocity. His fastball is special because he creates huge spin rates and significant carry coming from a low release height and flat approach angle. He utilizes it about 70 percent of the time while employing a tight upper-70s slider to throw off batters' timing. The extension in Rhudy's low-three-quarters delivery adds to his deception. He pounds the strike zone and ranked third in D-I in overall (72 percent) and fastball (77 percent) strike percentage. He's purely a reliever but his unhittable heater might make him a high-leverage option, especially if a pro team can help him gain more velocity.

A Wisconsin high school product, Burns began his college career by headlining Arizona State's rotation before shoulder tendinitis ended his freshman season after six starts. He has operated out of Texas' bullpen the last two years, impressing with his fastball but never throwing enough strikes to lock down the closer's role. He recorded a 5.64 ERA this season despite striking out 42 percent of the batters he faced. Burns parks at 95-98 mph and peaks at 100 with a fastball that plays even better than its velocity because of the riding action he creates coming out of a nearly over-the-top arm slot. His upper-80s cutter can be a plus pitch when it's on, but he almost never lands it for strikes, and it remains to be seen how effective it will be against pro hitters. His mid-80s changeup lacks life and often misses the zone so badly that it elicits few chases. The effort in Burns' delivery has resulted in a 16 percent walk rate in three college seasons. Though he's one of the more intriguing pure relievers in the Draft and possesses an explosive fastball, it will be hard to trust him in high-leverage situations unless he improves his well-below-average control and command. Few college pitchers can match his ability to get in-zone swings and misses with three different pitches, but he has so much difficulty finding the zone.

Mason McCraine's name popped up shortly before the 2025 Draft as a candidate to land a seven-figure bonus from a small group of teams, but he ultimately went unselected and headed to Auburn to play with older brother Brandon. The latter is a rare Draft-eligible redshirt freshman who couldn't get any playing time last spring before performing well in the Perfect Game Collegiate League during the summer. He began this year as a replacement for injured star Chris Rembert at second base before settling in at shortstop and leading the Tigers in hitting (.352) during the regular season. McCraine has a fluid right-handed stroke and a patient approach at the plate, though he can get too passive at times. He focuses on making line-drive contract from gap to gap but needs to add some muscle to his skinny 6-foot-3 frame and learn to turn on pitches and launch them in the air if he's going to tap into any power. His bat-to-ball skills didn't stand out as much in Southeastern Conference play, yet a team that believes in his projectable strength could envision him becoming a solid hitter with 12-15 homers per year and draft him as early as the fourth round if he's signable. A solid runner and athlete with arm strength to match, McCraine has a knack for stealing bases and the versatility to play all over the field. He has started games at shortstop, second base and third base this spring after manning right field and first base in the PGCL. He's a reliable defender at shortstop and will get a chance to show what he can do there in pro ball.
